title: The Electrical System — Alternator, Battery, and Electrical Failure

questions.text: In cruise at 8,500 feet in VFR conditions, the ammeter shows a sustained discharge even though the engine is running normally at 2,400 RPM. What has occurred and what is the immediate action?

options.label: A
options.text: The battery is failing — the discharge indication means the battery is delivering power but not receiving charge; this indicates a degraded battery that can no longer hold charge; the alternator is functioning normally; the battery should be replaced after landing but flight may continue normally since the alternator is primary

options.label: B
options.text: The alternator has failed — the engine-driven alternator is no longer producing electrical power; the battery is now the only source of electrical power for all aircraft systems; immediate actions: (1) attempt to reset the alternator (cycle the master switch or use the ALT FIELD circuit breaker if equipped); (2) if alternator does not restore, initiate load shedding (turn off non-essential electrical equipment); (3) advise ATC; (4) plan immediate diversion to the nearest airport before the battery depletes

options.label: C
options.text: The ammeter always shows discharge during radio transmission — the transmitter draws more current than the alternator produces for the duration of the transmission; if the discharge indication persists BETWEEN transmissions, then further investigation is warranted

options.label: D
options.text: The battery is fully charged and has stopped accepting charge current — the discharge indication is normal when the battery reaches 100% state of charge; the alternator has reduced output to maintenance level and the ammeter shows a small discharge as a result; no action required

questions.explanation: A sustained discharge on the ammeter in cruise — when the alternator should be providing more than adequate power — is the primary indicator of alternator failure. The alternator is the primary power source during engine-running operations. When it fails: all electrical loads (avionics, lights, pitot heat, COM radio, transponder) are drawing power directly from the battery. The battery's capacity is finite — typically 1-2 hours from full charge depending on total electrical load. In VFR conditions, this is serious but manageable. In IMC, it is an immediate emergency. The correct response sequence: (1) Attempt alternator reset per POH (some failures are transient — a master switch cycle or ALT circuit breaker cycle may restore output). (2) If reset fails, shed non-essential loads immediately (landing lights, position lights in daytime, non-critical avionics). (3) Contact ATC, request vectors to nearest airport, squawk 7700. (4) Estimate available battery time and compare to flight time to nearest airport. Option A invents a 'fully charged battery causing discharge indication' — a fully charged battery in normal operation simply does not receive charge current; the ammeter reads zero or very slight, not DISCHARGE. Option D mischaracterizes normal ammeter behavior — radio transmissions may MOMENTARILY dip the ammeter but should not produce sustained discharge in cruise.

questions.text: In IMC, the alternator fails at night. The pilot estimates 40 minutes of battery power remaining with current electrical load. The nearest IFR airport with an instrument approach is 55 minutes away. After shedding all non-essential loads, the pilot estimates 50 minutes of battery power. What is the correct course of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Declare an emergency immediately and divert to the nearest suitable VFR airport that can be reached within 50 minutes — even 50 minutes is close quarters for an IMC night flight with battery as sole power; if a VFR escape route is not available, declare emergency, squawk 7700, contact Center or Approach for immediate IFR vectors to the nearest airport with a serviceable approach; time the critical equipment carefully and consider turning off transponder (to save power) only as a last resort after ATC confirms they have you on radar

options.label: B
options.text: Continue to the destination — 50 minutes of battery after load shedding is close enough to the 55-minute flight time; with careful management, the pilot can make it to the destination; turning around adds additional flight time and may result in an empty battery before reaching any airport

options.label: C
options.text: Attempt to reset the alternator every 10 minutes — alternator faults typically clear themselves when the regulator cools down; three reset attempts over 30 minutes may restore alternator function before battery depletion; continue to destination while attempting resets

options.label: D
options.text: Continue to destination and use idle electrical load management — turn off the transponder and secondary COM radio; use only one COM for communication; the remaining essential loads (attitude indicator, primary COM, GPS) draw less than 5 amps; at 5 amps draw from a 17 AH battery, the remaining power is over 3 hours, far exceeding the 55-minute flight time

questions.explanation: The math: 50 minutes battery power vs. 55 minutes to destination = 5-minute deficit with zero margin. In IMC at night, this is an emergency. The 5-minute gap assumes: (a) the battery capacity estimate is accurate (estimates carry ±15% uncertainty), (b) all shed loads stay shed and no unforeseen load appears, (c) no delays, holding, or extended approach clearances at destination. In real IMC night operations, all three assumptions can be violated. A 5-minute buffer on battery power in IMC is not a safety margin — it is a lottery. The correct action: DECLARE EMERGENCY NOW while radio and transponder still have full power. ATC with 50 minutes of battery notice can provide: (1) Immediate IFR vectors to the nearest airport — not the destination, but the nearest airport with a serviceable approach. (2) Emergency handling priority (no sequencing delays). (3) Emergency equipment standby at the airport. (4) Coordination of the landing without communications if battery depletes. Declaring now with 50 minutes of power is significantly safer than declaring in 5 minutes with 45 remaining when the destination is still 50 minutes away. Option A rationalizes the 5-minute shortfall as manageable — in IMC at night this is the Invulnerability cognitive trap that causes fatal accidents.

questions.text: In cruise, a pilot detects an electrical burning smell and notices a wisp of smoke from behind the instrument panel. The pilot's FIRST action should be:

options.label: A
options.text: Pull all circuit breakers in sequence from left to right until the smoke stops — systematically removing power from individual circuits identifies the source and isolates it without losing all electrical power and navigation capability

options.label: B
options.text: Attempt to identify the source of the smoke before taking any action — pulling circuit breakers or turning off the master switch without knowing the source may disable critical flight instruments; locate and isolate the specific Circuit breaker before taking further action

options.label: C
options.text: Turn off the MASTER SWITCH, then the AVIONICS MASTER simultaneously — removing all electrical power immediately is the highest priority to eliminate the power source feeding the electrical fire; trying to identify the source introduces delay while the fire may spread

options.label: D
options.text: Open all cockpit ventilation immediately and squawk 7700 — fresh air ventilation is the most effective initial action for smoke in the cockpit; the transponder squawk ensures ATC knows the situation before any further troubleshooting

questions.explanation: In-flight electrical fire procedure is a MEMORY EMERGENCY — it requires immediate action without reference to a checklist, because the fire is developing in real time. The first action is MASTER SWITCH OFF (and avionics master if separate). Rationale: (1) Electrical fires are fed by current through the fault. Removing electrical power removes the fuel for the fire. (2) Every second of delay with power ON allows the fire to grow, melt more insulation, possibly ignite adjacent materials. (3) Flight controls and engine are MECHANICAL — they do not require electrical power to function (in most light single-engine aircraft with vacuum-powered AI and engine magneto ignition). The aircraft can still be flown after the master switch is off. Note: in glass-cockpit aircraft with all-electric flight instruments, the emergency is more complex — consult aircraft-specific POH. Option A ('identify the source first') introduces a fatal delay. Option C (ventilate first) is STEP FOUR, not step one — ventilating with the fault still powered accelerates combustion. Option D (pull breakers sequentially) is logical but too slow — individual CB identification during an active fire takes 30-60 seconds; master off takes 1 second.

questions.text: During cruise at 6,500 feet, the COM 1 circuit breaker trips. The pilot loses COM 1. COM 2 is functional. A passenger asks: 'Just push the button back in — why not reset it?' What is the correct response and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Do not reset — a tripped circuit breaker indicates current in that circuit exceeded the breaker's rated capacity, meaning a fault exists; resetting it may re-close an active fault, causing the wire insulation to heat and potentially start an electrical fire; with COM 2 available for communication, COM 1 is not safety-critical in this specific scenario; the breaker should remain open and the fault investigated by an A&P after landing

options.label: B
options.text: Reset it — circuit breakers on certified aircraft are designed for in-flight reset; a COM radio circuit breaker is a critical communication system; resetting it is required under 14 CFR 91.205 which mandates that all required communication equipment be functional during flight operations

options.label: C
options.text: Reset it once, and once only — 14 CFR 91.0 allows a single in-flight reset attempt for communication equipment breakers only; communication equipment has a statutory exception to the no-reset rule; apply only ONE reset attempt and if it trips again, leave it open

options.label: D
options.text: Reset it after a 5-minute cooling delay — circuit breakers sometimes trip from momentary overload rather than sustained faults; a 5-minute cooling period allows thermal resetting; the trip was likely a transient and the circuit is probably healthy; resetting after cooling is standard procedure per AC 43.13-1B

questions.explanation: The standard guidance on in-flight circuit breaker reset: Do NOT reset a tripped breaker unless required for safety. The rationale: a circuit breaker trips when current in the circuit exceeds its rated capacity. This happens because: (a) There is a short circuit (damaged wire contacting ground), or (b) The load connected to that circuit exceeded its rated draw (failing avionics drawing excess current). Resetting re-closes the circuit to the same fault. If a wire is shorted, resetting brings full current back through it — the wire heats, insulation melts, potentially igniting. In this scenario, COM 2 is functional for communication needs. COM 1 is not safety-critical in this context. The breaker remains open. Land and have an A&P investigate the cause. Exception: if COM 1 were the ONLY radio and the pilot needed it for ATC communication in controlled airspace or IFR flight — then ONE reset attempt per the POH could be justified; if it trips again, leave it open. Option A invents a 14 CFR 91.205 mandate to reset tripped breakers — the regulation requires communication equipment to be functional, but does not require re-energizing faulty circuits. Option D references a non-existent '14 CFR 91.0' — no such section exists.

questions.text: Before starting the engine, the student asks why the POH instructs the pilot to turn the AVIONICS MASTER to OFF before engine start, then turn it ON after the engine is running. What is the correct explanation?

options.label: A
options.text: The sequence is purely traditional — early avionics used vacuum tube technology that required 5-10 minutes of warm-up time; the modern 'avionics on after engine start' sequence is historical convention that no longer has technical relevance but remains in POHs for regulatory continuity

options.label: B
options.text: During engine start, the starter motor draws very high current (150-300 amps), causing bus voltage to drop significantly (from 12V to 8-9V) for several seconds; this low-voltage transient can damage sensitive avionics equipment; keeping the avionics master OFF during start protects the radios, glass displays, and autopilot from voltage spikes and drops; once the engine is running and the alternator restores bus voltage, the avionics master is turned on

options.label: C
options.text: The avionics master must be off during start because starting the engine with avionics on causes the engine computer to record a fault code; the fault code disables the autopilot for the next flight as a safety measure until cleared by maintenance

options.label: D
options.text: The avionics master is turned off before engine start because the magnetos operate on the same electrical bus as the avionics; with both on simultaneously, grounding interference between the magneto P-leads and the avionics shielding can cause a hot magneto fault; separation during start prevents this interaction

questions.explanation: This is a systems-knowledge question with a specific, verifiable technical answer. Modern avionics (glass displays, GPS units, digital COM radios, autopilots) contain sensitive microprocessors and power supply circuits designed to operate within a specific voltage range (typically 10-16V DC). During engine start: the starter motor draws 150-300 amps momentarily, causing the bus voltage to sag from the normal 12-13V down to 8-9V or lower. This voltage drop can corrupt microprocessor memory, reset GPS databases, or damage power supply regulators inside avionics units. Additionally, when the starter motor is interrupted and the alternator comes online, there can be brief voltage SPIKES above 14V. The avionics master switch is specifically positioned to isolate avionics from the main bus during this transient period. The sequence: avionics master OFF → start engine → confirm alternator online (ammeter shows charge) → turn avionics master ON → normal bus voltage to avionics. Option A invents an 'engine computer fault code' system that does not exist in piston light aircraft. Option D incorrectly attributes the sequence to historical vacuum tube legacy — modern glass-cockpit aircraft have eliminated vacuum tubes but maintain the same avionics master off-for-start sequence for solid-state electronics protection.

questions.text: After turning the master switch OFF during a smoke-in-cockpit emergency, the smoke STOPS within 60 seconds. The pilot is at 7,000 feet, 15 miles from the departure airport in VFR conditions. The pilot considers restoring electrical power to use the radio to advise ATC. What is the safest course of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Land immediately without restoring any electrical power — in VFR at 7,000 feet, 15 miles from the airport, the pilot can visually navigate to the airport and execute a no-radio landing; the remaining flight is short and safe without any electrical power; only restore master if essential to safety of the landing itself (landing lights if night)

options.label: B
options.text: Restore all electrical power immediately — the smoke has stopped confirming the issue was an electrical fault that has self-resolved; with master ON, use COM radio and GPS to navigate to the nearest airport for inspection

options.label: C
options.text: Restore ONLY the COM radio and transponder (if on a separate switch or controllable via breaker) — the smoke stopping with master off confirms the fault was electrical; to contact ATC, a careful partial power restoration may be justified; turn on avionics master or COM breaker ONLY, monitor for smoke recurrence, squawk 7700, advise ATC, navigate VMC to nearest airport visually; do NOT restore non-essential loads; land as soon as possible for full inspection

options.label: D
options.text: Wait 10 minutes before restoring power — electrical faults in avionics self-clear after a cooling period; restoring after 10 minutes of off-time allows the fault to reset thermally; if smoke does not recur after restore, the aircraft is safe to fly to the planned destination and have the fault investigated at leisure

questions.explanation: After an electrical fire/smoke event with master switched off and smoke stopping, the situation is: (1) An electrical fault exists somewhere in the airplane — the smoke confirmed this. (2) The aircraft is flyable without electrical power (VFR, VMC, magneto ignition). (3) The nearest airport is reachable visually. (4) ATC notification and coordination would improve safety but requires partial power restoration. The staged approach (Option B): restore COM/transponder only, monitor closely for smoke recurrence, squawk 7700, advise ATC, navigate visually, land. This gives the pilot ATC coordination and tracking while minimizing the re-energized fault risk. Option C is also defensible — in VFR conditions 15 miles from an airport, a no-radio landing is achievable and avoids re-energizing any fault. Option C may actually be safer than B if the pilot is uncertain which circuit caused the fault. Both B and C represent good airmanship. Option A (restore all power) re-closes ALL potential faults simultaneously and has caused secondary electrical fires in GA accident records. Option D (10-minute thermal reset) invents a self-clearing mechanism for electrical faults — short circuits do not thermally heal; the fault remains until physically repaired.
questions.sjt_rationale: The NTSB record shows secondary electrical fires after initial master-off recovery as a pattern in smoke-in-cockpit accidents. The 'smoke stopped = fixed' conclusion is incomplete — the fault still exists; only the power source was removed. The safest ADM: do the minimum electrical restoration required for safety, get on the ground, and let an A&P find the fault.

questions.text: Alternator failure occurs in night IMC. Current electrical draw with all radios, GPS, transponder, pitot heat, and position lights on is estimated at 22 amps. Battery capacity is approximately 17 AH at 80% state of charge (13.6 AH usable). After shedding position lights (1.5A) and DME (0.5A), the load drops to 20 amps. Estimated time to nearest IFR airport is 38 minutes. Is the battery capacity sufficient to reach the airport?

options.label: A
options.text: The battery capacity question is irrelevant — once the alternator fails, the regulations require the pilot to declare an emergency regardless of battery capacity remaining; 14 CFR 91.7 mandates immediate emergency declaration and landing upon alternator failure in IMC

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — the pilot has a 2.8-minute battery margin which is adequate by FAA standards; 14 CFR 91.185 requires only that aircraft have electrical power for navigation lights and communication equipment; the 40.8-minute calculated duration satisfies this requirement with positive margin

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — 13.6 AH ÷ 20A = 40.8 minutes; this exceeds the 38-minute flight time; there is a 2.8-minute margin which, combined with the battery typically delivering 10% beyond the rated AH at low temperatures, provides adequate safety margin

options.label: D
options.text: No — 13.6 AH ÷ 20A = 40.8 minutes theoretical; however, this margin (2.8 minutes) is dangerously thin for night IMC; battery capacity estimates carry ±15% uncertainty; actual usable capacity could be as low as 11.6 AH → 11.6 ÷ 20 = 34.6 minutes — shorter than the 38-minute flight time; the pilot should declare emergency immediately, request direct routing to reduce flight time, shed additional loads (position lights in IMC have reduced value — ATC has radar), and target a 10-minute or greater margin

questions.explanation: This question requires correctly applying battery math with appropriate uncertainty margins. Calculated battery time: 13.6 AH ÷ 20A = 40.8 minutes. But the safety question is whether this is ENOUGH given the uncertainty. A 2.8-minute margin (7%) is insufficient given: (1) Battery AH capacity estimates have ±10-20% uncertainty depending on battery age, temperature, and discharge rate. (2) At 20A discharge, the battery may deliver less than rated AH (Peukert's Law — high discharge rates reduce effective capacity). (3) Flight time estimates assume no delays, direct routing, and standard approach — IMC approaches routinely add 5-10 minutes. (4) If the battery capacity is 10% lower than estimated: 13.6 × 0.90 = 12.2 AH → 12.2 ÷ 20 = 36.6 minutes — shorter than the 38-minute trip. Correct actions: (1) Declare emergency NOW — getting on the emergency frequency while you have 40 minutes of power is far more effective than declaring in 5 minutes. (2) Request direct routing — shorten the 38-minute estimate. (3) Shed additional loads — position lights in IMC at night: ATC has radar; reduce to min essential (COM, transponder, GPS, pitot heat only). Options: shedding position lights: saves 1.5A. At 18.5A: 13.6 ÷ 18.5 = 43.5 minutes with a 5.5-minute margin — still thin. Request direct and declare emergency.

questions.text: A pilot notices a slight discharge on the ammeter shortly after engine start while taxiing. After reaching cruise RPM (1,000 RPM), the ammeter still shows a slight discharge. Is this normal?

options.label: A
options.text: No — by 1,000 RPM (cruise taxi RPM), the alternator should be producing enough voltage to power the avionics and charge the battery; sustained discharge at 1,000 RPM on the ground after engine stabilization indicates a possible alternator or voltage regulator issue that should be investigated before flight

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — the ammeter always shows discharge until both radios are tuned and the NAV equipment is receiving a station; the avionics draw is suppressed during tuning; once all radios are set to active frequencies, the ammeter transitions to zero or slight charge

options.label: C
options.text: Not necessarily — the ammeter shows discharge immediately after engine start because the starter motor drained the battery; the battery requires 5-10 minutes of engine operation at any RPM to return to full charge; the ammeter will transition to charge automatically after the battery recharges

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — the ammeter always shows discharge at low RPM because the alternator only produces full output above approximately 1,200-1,500 RPM; slight discharge during taxi at 1,000 RPM is normal and expected; the ammeter should transition to charge after takeoff at full power RPM

questions.explanation: This question requires understanding the alternator output vs. RPM relationship. The aircraft alternator is an engine-driven AC generator with output voltage proportional to rotational speed. Most aircraft alternators begin producing useful charge voltage at approximately 800-1,200 engine RPM — the exact threshold depends on the alternator design and belt/gear drive ratio. At typical ground idle (600-700 RPM), the alternator may produce little to no usable charge output. At taxi power (900-1,100 RPM), the alternator is approaching but may not be at full output. A slight discharge at 1,000 RPM on the ground is typically normal if: (a) the avionics are active (drawing current), and (b) the alternator is at the low end of its output range. The ammeter should transition to CHARGE as RPM increases toward 1,200+ (ground test RPM during runup). If the ammeter STILL shows discharge at runup RPM (1,700-1,800), that would indicate alternator failure. This is a key reason the runup includes an alternator/electrical check — to confirm the system is functioning before flight. Option B would be concerning only if the discharge persists at runup/higher RPM. Option D describes recharging in terms of minutes — this is partially accurate (the battery was drained by starting), but the key point is that at 1,000 RPM the alternator output may be below the electrical load demand.
